r1_cat.title: Milo the Cat
r1_cat.text:
Milo is a small grey cat. He lives with Sam in a yellow house by the park.

Every morning Milo sits on the window ledge and watches the birds. When Sam comes downstairs, Milo runs to his bowl and miaows very loudly until he is fed.

Milo's favourite place to sleep is the big blue chair. Sam is not allowed to sit there any more.

r1_park.title: A Day at the Park
r1_park.text:
On Saturday, Priya went to the park with her dad. She took her red scooter.

First they fed the ducks with some old bread. Then Priya went on the swings six times. She counted every one.

It started to rain, so they ran home. Priya's socks were wet but she did not mind. She had a hot chocolate and told her mum all about the ducks.

r2_lighthouse.title: The Lighthouse Keeper
r2_lighthouse.text:
Grace lived in a tall white lighthouse on a rocky island. Her job was to keep the great lamp burning all night so that ships did not crash on the rocks.

One stormy night the wind howled so hard that the windows rattled. Grace heard a sound she had never heard before: a bell, ringing out at sea. A ship was in trouble.

Grace pulled on her heavy coat and rowed out into the waves. It took her a very long time, but she brought nine cold, frightened sailors safely back to the island. She gave them blankets and hot soup, and then she climbed the stairs to check the lamp was still burning.

In the morning the storm had gone. The sailors said Grace was the bravest person they had ever met. Grace said she had only done her job.

r2_seeds.title: How Seeds Travel
r2_seeds.text:
Plants cannot walk, but their seeds can travel a long way.

Some seeds have tiny parachutes. A dandelion seed floats away on the wind and can land in the next field.

Other seeds hide inside sweet fruit. A bird eats a juicy blackberry and flies off. Later the seeds come out in the bird's droppings, far from where the plant was growing.

A few seeds are sticky or hooked. Burdock seeds catch on the fur of a passing fox, or on your socks, and drop off somewhere new.

Why bother travelling? If all the seeds landed under the parent plant, there would not be enough light or water for them all to grow.

r3_anning.title: The Girl Who Found Dragons
r3_anning.text:
In the early 1800s, a girl called Mary Anning walked along the cliffs at Lyme Regis in Dorset, searching the beach after storms. Her family was poor, and Mary sold the curious stone shells she found to visitors for a few pennies.

One day, when she was about twelve, Mary and her brother uncovered something extraordinary: an enormous skull with rows of pointed teeth, buried in the rock. Over the following months Mary carefully chipped away at the cliff until she had freed the whole seventeen-foot skeleton. People called it a sea dragon. Today we call it an ichthyosaur.

Mary went on to find many more remarkable fossils. Scientists travelled from London to buy them and to ask her questions, because nobody understood the Dorset rocks better than she did. Yet because she was a woman, and not wealthy, Mary was not allowed to join the Geological Society, and other people's names appeared on the scientific papers her discoveries made possible.

Mary Anning died in 1847. It took more than a hundred years for the world to give her the credit she had earned. Her fossils are still on display in museums today, and her story changed what people believed about the history of life on Earth.

r3_bees.title: Why Bees Matter
r3_bees.text:
A single honeybee may visit five thousand flowers in one day. It is not being helpful on purpose. It is looking for nectar, a sugary liquid it takes back to the hive to make honey.

As the bee pushes into each flower, sticky yellow pollen catches on the tiny hairs covering its body. When the bee moves to the next flower, some of that pollen brushes off. This is pollination, and without it most flowering plants could not make seeds.

Roughly one mouthful in every three that we eat depends on pollinating insects. Apples, strawberries, beans, tomatoes and almonds all need them. Wheat does not, because it is pollinated by the wind.

Bee numbers have fallen sharply. Farmers now grow fewer wildflowers, and some pesticides harm bees. You can help by planting lavender or borage, by leaving a patch of your garden to grow wild, and by never disturbing a hive.
